## The measoshapes package

```r
remotes::install_github("AustralianAntarcticDivision/measoshapes")
library(measoshapes)
```

The package has the regions as [sf](https://r-spatial.github.io/sf/) data sets, one row per region
(20 rows), with columns `name`, `label`, `sector`, `zone` and `fill`:

* `measo_regions06`, `measo_regions06_coastline`: polar equal area
* `measo_regions06_ll`, `measo_regions06_ll_coastline`: longitude/latitude
* `measo_names06`: the columns alone

```{r}
measo_regions06
```

Version 05 is in the package as released (`measo_regions05` etc., 24 rows with the West Pacific regions
in two pieces, and `measo_names` row-aligned with them); see the
[README](https://github.com/AustralianAntarcticDivision/measoshapes#version-05).

The files on the [Data](data.qmd) page (one row per region) are in the package too:

```r
f <- system.file("extdata/measo_regions06.parquet", package = "measoshapes")
```

## Reading from a URL

No package installation is needed to read the published files. GDAL reads them directly from the URL.

```r
u <- "https://australianantarcticdivision.github.io/measoshapes/data/v06/measo_regions06.parquet"

## sf
x <- sf::read_sf(u)

## terra
v <- terra::vect(u)

## gdalraster
lyr <- gdalraster::GDALVector$new(paste0("/vsicurl/", u))
d <- lyr$fetch(-1)
lyr$close()

## arrow, geometry as well-known binary (wk/geoarrow)
library(geoarrow)
tab <- arrow::read_parquet(u)
```

FlatGeobuf and GeoJSON work the same way (change the file name), and are a good choice if your GDAL
doesn't have the Parquet driver (check `"Parquet" %in% sf::st_drivers()$name`).

## Assigning regions to data

To find the region for longitude/latitude locations, transform them to the polar equal area projection
and join with the polar regions:

```{r}
regions <- read_sf(file.path(dd, "measo_regions06.parquet"))  ## or the URL above
pts <- data.frame(lon = c(147.3, 100.5, -10.5, -82.5, 171.5, -175.5),
                  lat = c(-50.2, -60.5, -70.5, -45.5, -65.5, -65.5))
p <- st_as_sf(pts, coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = "OGC:CRS84", remove = FALSE)
p <- st_join(st_transform(p, st_crs(regions)), regions)
st_drop_geometry(p)
```

The polar regions are densified to 0.2° from the longitude/latitude definition, so this agrees with the
definition except for locations within a very short distance of a boundary.

For gridded data, the same applies: classify cell centres, or rasterize the polar regions onto your grid
(e.g. `terra::rasterize(terra::vect(regions), grid, field = "name")`).

## Maps

```{r}
#| label: fig-r-map
#| fig-cap: "Base graphics with the fill colours."
par(mar = rep(0, 4))
plot(st_geometry(regions), col = regions$fill, border = "grey60")
```

With ggplot2, use the colours as they are with `scale_fill_identity()`:

```r
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(regions, aes(fill = fill)) + geom_sf(colour = "grey60") + scale_fill_identity()
```
